transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Thank you for making time on short notice. As you know, Harbor Point Properties has come to us with a restructuring request on their $8 million term loan. Before I make a decision, I need each of you to walk me through your assessment of the proposal. They're asking for three things: a 12-month maturity extension, a waiver of the current financial covenant, and release of $900,000 of equipment collateral. Let's go through the standard agenda -- risk, relationship coverage, legal, and collateral management. Who'd like to start?

transcript.text: Good morning, Elena. I'll start on the risk assessment. I've been reviewing the covenant testing file this week, and there are a few critical findings the committee needs to hear before any decision is made. First, Harbor Point's leverage is currently 0.3x above the permitted level -- so the covenant breach is real and measurable. Second, our workout policy is specific about what we can offer in response: it allows a waiver, but only with a 9-month extension, not the 12 months they're requesting, and it requires a monthly leverage certificate going forward. Third, I have not yet attached the testing file to the committee package, so I want to make sure everyone has visibility into these findings now. In short, from a risk perspective, we can accommodate a restructuring, but not on the terms as proposed -- the extension needs to be capped at 9 months, and we need monthly leverage reporting as a condition of the waiver. I also have concerns about the collateral release request, but I'll defer to collateral management on that piece. Let me go ahead and formally share these findings with the group.

transcript.text: Elena, before we move on, I want to make sure the committee package is complete. I noted earlier that I hadn't yet attached the covenant testing file to the committee package -- I'll make sure that gets done today so all findings are formally documented. On the equipment collateral release, I deferred to collateral management, and I'm glad Nadia is being asked to weigh in. I'll defer to Nadia's specific findings on the equipment valuation, but from a risk standpoint, I'd want to see strong justification before agreeing to any collateral release in this restructuring.

transcript.text: From a relationship coverage perspective, I want to weigh in on the equipment collateral release question Elena raised. The $1,200,000 equity injection I disclosed is a significant commitment from the owners -- it demonstrates their willingness to put fresh capital into the deal at closing. That said, Jonas makes a fair point about reducing our collateral cushion during a period of heightened oversight. I'd want to understand from Nadia whether the equipment being released is depreciating or underperforming as collateral, and whether the equity injection plus the remaining collateral base provides adequate coverage even with the $900,000 release. If the equipment is the weakest link in the collateral package after receivables, releasing it while retaining stronger collateral and adding $1.2 million in new equity might actually clean up the collateral position. But that's a question for Nadia's review to answer. I'd also note that from a relationship standpoint, the owners have been proactive -- they signed the term sheet and committed new equity before we even asked, which suggests they're motivated to make this work.

transcript.text: Before any decision is made on the equipment collateral release, I need to flag a critical legal issue. I confirmed while reviewing the intercreditor agreement this week that the senior lender must give written consent before any equipment collateral is released. That consent has not yet been requested. This means we cannot proceed with the $900,000 equipment collateral release -- or even commit to it in restructuring terms -- until we obtain that written consent from the senior lender. This is a binding requirement under the intercreditor agreement, and failing to obtain consent before releasing collateral would put the bank in breach of that agreement.

transcript.text: Thank you, Rafael -- that's a critical legal constraint, and I appreciate you flagging it. From a collateral management perspective, let me address the equipment release question directly. My collateral review yesterday focused on the receivables, which I've already flagged as the weakest and most volatile part of the package. I want to be transparent with the committee: my review did not include a specific valuation assessment of the $900,000 equipment collateral being proposed for release. So I cannot provide a definitive answer today on whether that equipment is depreciating, underperforming, or whether releasing it would leave us with adequate coverage. What I can say is this: given that receivables already require weekly monitoring due to their weakness, releasing $900,000 of equipment collateral on top of that would reduce our overall collateral cushion at a time when we're tightening oversight. I'd want to complete a dedicated equipment valuation review before supporting any release. Combined with Rafael's point that we can't proceed without senior lender consent anyway, my recommendation is that the equipment release should not be approved in this restructuring unless and until we have both the senior lender's written consent and a completed equipment valuation showing the remaining collateral base -- including Mei's $1.2 million equity injection -- provides adequate coverage. In the meantime, the weekly borrowing-base certificate on receivables and the monitoring schedule update I flagged earlier would still be required conditions of any extension.
